The salt reached the back of Garen's throat before the ladle finished its pour. A fine grit rode the wind, caught in his teeth, and tasted of cold minerals and burned offerings. He walked the inner ring of the Ashfall Stair landing with the bone ladle held level, laying a fresh white ribbon inside the iron stanchions, and the old basalt drank it the way it drank everything, without comment. Somewhere above the soot the Ashfall bell finished counting six strokes of morning, each one arriving down the stairwell flattened and late. First writ-day of the waning moon. Late autumn. The purge-list carried four names, and one of them would be served on this terrace.

The wind was *tobhandari*, wet soot off the slag-hills, and it plucked at the ribbon's edge while he worked. Beneath his boot soles the Spire breathed, a long mechanical draw and a longer release, deep enough to reach him through leather. Years of it had worn the noticing down to nothing, but purge mornings gave it back. The breathing was why the salt went down fresh every writ-day. Its stanchions were iron to the root.

He racked the kit on a fold of oiled cloth at the second stanchion. Thirty links of *bhandari*-chain, cold-forged, each stamped with the Ashfall mark. Nine vials of consecrated salt in their wooden rack. The purge-writ in its lead tube, and the sealing-tongs beside it. He counted the links by touch, thumb over stamp, twice through, because a binder who trusted another man's rack was a binder with a short career. The tongs he checked for true. The tube he did not open yet.

"Captain Orvell."

She stood at the fourth stone past the line, ledger under her arm, canvas apron already gray with the morning's sootfall. "Aye."

"Witness stands at the third stone. Ledger open, iron off the hands." He waited until she had moved the two paces left and thumbed the pages apart. "A binding without a living witness is heresy, and worse, it fails. If you look away at any point, say so now and I'll hold the writ."

"I'll look where you point me, Commander." She set the ledger flat on her forearm. "For the record before you start: salt poured, two measures even. Vials racked, nine, one short a stopper, and I signed for that stopper at fifth bell. Effects held in trust from the cell, three items, sealed bag. You'll have my countersign before the cart rolls."

"Good."

Dax Ferren came up the stair without greeting anyone. The Spire's salt-auditor was a spare man with ink to the second knuckle and a brass jeweler's scale in a felt-lined box, its pans no wider than thumbnails. He crouched at the ribbon's hem, pinched up three grains, weighed them with the box braced on his knee, and put one on his tongue. His ledger rode pushed
